prompt: Why do plane-wave codes like VASP describe orbitals as a sum of waves?

options.text: Waves of fixed wavelength form a simple, systematic basis: more waves give a better answer, and nothing depends on where the atoms are
options.why: That is the key advantage: one number, the cutoff, controls the quality for every atom type.

options.text: Because electrons in crystals really are free plane waves
options.why: Tempting, but the orbitals are not free waves. The waves are only a convenient set of building blocks.

options.text: Because plane waves need no pseudopotential
options.why: The reverse: plane waves need a smooth potential, which is why pseudopotentials are used.

Ask what you change to get a more accurate answer.

prompt: In a plane-wave calculation, which waves are kept in the basis?

options.text: Those whose kinetic energy is at most the cutoff
options.why: The cutoff sets a maximum kinetic energy; every wave below it is included.

options.text: Those whose wavelength is exactly the cell length
options.why: Only a few waves would fit that rule, and the basis would be far too small.

options.text: Those that overlap an atom
options.why: The basis does not depend on atom positions; all waves under the cutoff are kept.

hints: The cutoff is an energy.
Waves with larger wave vector have more kinetic energy.

options.text: It becomes twice as large

options.text: It stays the same
options.why: Shorter waves are more strongly curved, so they carry more kinetic energy.

prompt: What does a higher ENCUT do to a calculation?

options.text: Includes more plane waves: the result gets more accurate and the run gets slower
options.why: It is a straight trade of cost for accuracy, until the result stops changing.

options.text: Makes the SCF loop converge faster
options.why: The cutoff changes the basis, not the mixing, so convergence speed is not what it controls.

options.text: Moves the Fermi level
options.why: The Fermi level is set by the electrons and bands, not by the size of the basis.

hints: ENCUT is the largest kinetic energy included.

prompt: Why does a VASP run need a set of k-points, rather than one calculation?

options.text: Quantities such as the density are averages over all k in the Brillouin zone, and the average is approximated by a finite sample
options.why: The sum over an infinite crystal becomes a sum over a few chosen k.

options.text: Each k-point is a different atom
options.why: k labels waves in reciprocal space, not atoms.

options.text: Each k-point is a separate ionic step
options.why: k-points are sampled within one SCF step, not across the relaxation.

options.text: The set of all occupied states

prompt: What is the purpose of smearing in a metal calculation?

options.why: Only Fermi-Dirac smearing corresponds to a physical temperature, and the others are numerical aids.

options.text: To remove the Fermi level
options.why: The Fermi level remains; only the step at it is blurred.

prompt: Cubic SrTiO3 has the space group Pm-3m. What does the first letter, P, tell you?

options.text: The lattice is primitive: there are no extra centring points
options.why: The first letter of a Hermann-Mauguin symbol is the centring type, and P means primitive.

options.text: The structure is a perovskite
options.why: Tempting for SrTiO3, but the letter describes the lattice centring, and many non-perovskites have P groups.

options.text: The group contains a mirror plane
options.why: Mirrors are the m symbols that follow the letter.

options.text: The lattice is face-centred
options.why: Face-centred is F, as in Fm-3m for rock salt.

hints: The symbol starts with one capital letter followed by symmetry elements.
Compare Pm-3m with Fm-3m for NaCl.

visual.caption: Cubic perovskite SrTiO3 in its cubic cell.
visual.alt: Strontium at the corners of a cube and titanium at the centre inside an octahedron of six oxygen atoms.

prompt: A 4 by 4 by 4 Gamma-centred mesh is used on a simple cubic crystal with the full cubic point group (48 operations: every sign change and every swap of the axes). How many irreducible k-points remain?
hints: Along each axis the coordinates are 0, 1/4, 1/2 and -1/4, and a sign change maps -1/4 onto 1/4.
Swaps of the axes mean only the unordered set of three values from 0, 1/4 and 1/2 matters.

visual.caption: A 4 by 4 Gamma-centred mesh in one plane of a square reciprocal cell.
visual.alt: Sixteen k-points on a square grid that includes the centre of the reciprocal cell.

prompt: VASP stops with "inverse of rotation matrix was not found (increase SYMPREC)" on a cubic structure taken from an earlier relaxation. What is the likely cause and the first fix?

options.text: The positions are slightly off their symmetric sites; symmetrize the structure or raise SYMPREC to about 1E-4
options.why: The Workflow Handbook names this message for positions that are nearly, but not exactly, symmetric; a symmetrized file or a looser tolerance lets the search succeed.

options.text: The POTCAR does not match the POSCAR
options.why: A wrong POTCAR causes other trouble; the symmetry search only uses the lattice, the positions and MAGMOM.

options.text: Every cubic crystal needs ISYM = -1
options.why: Switching off symmetry hides the message but costs the full k-mesh and leaves the noisy structure as it is.

options.text: The k-mesh is too coarse
options.why: The mesh is reduced after the symmetry search; this error comes from the search itself.

hints: The message names a tolerance.
What can be slightly wrong about a structure that came out of a relaxation?

items.label: Symmetry search with the tolerance SYMPREC

visual.caption: Where the symmetry search sits in a VASP run.
visual.alt: A four-step flow from POSCAR through the symmetry search and the k-point reduction to the electronic loop, with the symmetry search highlighted.

prompt: You relax a six-layer slab with 15 angstrom of vacuum. Which ISIF should you use?

options.text: ISIF = 2: the ions relax and the cell stays fixed
options.why: The in-plane lattice comes from the bulk and the vacuum must keep its size, so only the ions should move.

options.text: ISIF = 3: ions, shape and volume
options.why: Tempting because it is the full relaxation, but vacuum has nothing to push back, so the cell collapses along the normal.

options.text: ISIF = 4: ions and shape at fixed volume
options.why: The shape may then change, so the vacuum can shrink while the in-plane lattice stretches.

options.text: ISIF = 7: volume only
options.why: Changing the volume scales the vacuum and the in-plane lattice together, which is not wanted for a slab.

hints: What resists a change of cell size along the vacuum direction?
Which ISIF keeps the cell exactly as built?

visual.caption: A cell with its atoms before a relaxation.
visual.alt: A parallelogram cell with atoms inside, drawn before any change of atoms, shape or volume.

prompt: Why does a tight force criterion such as EDIFFG = -0.001 need a tight EDIFF such as 1E-7 or 1E-8?

options.text: Forces from a loosely converged density are noisy, so the ions chatter around the minimum and never meet the criterion
options.why: Forces are derivatives that depend on the converged density; noise in them larger than the criterion keeps the relaxation from stopping.

options.text: EDIFFG is measured in units of EDIFF
options.why: A negative EDIFFG is a force in eV per angstrom; it has its own units.

options.text: A tight EDIFF makes each ionic step longer
options.why: The step length is set by the algorithm and POTIM, not by EDIFF.

options.text: VASP refuses to start otherwise
options.why: VASP starts, but the relaxation may run to NSW without converging.

hints: Where do the forces come from?
What happens to a stopping test when the quantity it tests is noisy?

visual.caption: The largest force at each ionic step, with the stop line of the force criterion.
visual.alt: Falling points of the largest force on a logarithmic axis, crossing a horizontal stop line.

prompt: An ISIF = 3 relaxation reports "reached required accuracy", but the volume changed by several percent. Why copy CONTCAR to POSCAR and run again?

options.text: VASP kept the plane-wave basis of the starting volume, so the new cell carries Pulay stress; rerun until it converges in 1 to 3 steps
options.why: The basis is set up at the start of a run; after a large volume change it no longer matches the cutoff, and the rerun rebuilds it.

options.text: CONTCAR only becomes a valid structure after a rerun
options.why: CONTCAR is a valid POSCAR at every step; the issue is the basis, not the file.

options.text: The first run did not compute forces on its last step
options.why: Forces and stress are computed at every ionic step.

options.text: A rerun refines the k-mesh automatically
options.why: The k-mesh comes from KPOINTS or KSPACING and does not change between runs on its own.

hints: What stays fixed in VASP during one run while the cell changes?
What is Pulay stress caused by?

items.label: Static run on the final structure

visual.caption: The relax and rerun loop of the Workflow Handbook.
visual.alt: A four-step flow: relax the cell, copy CONTCAR to POSCAR, relax again, then a static run; the second relaxation is highlighted.

prompt: You relax a perfectly cubic perovskite whose true ground state has tilted octahedra. The run ends with near-zero forces and a cubic cell. What happened?

options.text: By symmetry the forces that would tilt the octahedra are exactly zero, so it stopped on a saddle point; rattle the atoms or lower the symmetry and relax again
options.why: VASP keeps the starting space group, and in a symmetric structure every force that would break the symmetry vanishes, even on top of an energy ridge.

options.text: Zero forces prove that the cubic structure is the ground state
options.why: Forces vanish at every stationary point: minima, maxima and saddle points alike.

options.text: EDIFFG was too tight
options.why: A tighter criterion only stops closer to the stationary point; it does not create symmetry.

options.text: ISIF = 3 forbids tilts
options.why: ISIF chooses whether the cell may change; it does not remove degrees of freedom of the ions.

hints: Can a force that breaks a symmetry appear in a perfectly symmetric structure?
Are minima the only places where forces vanish?

The slope is the energy change divided by the displacement.
